clinical.Title: CLINICAL EXAMINATION
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: Instructions: Answer all sub-questions carefully.

clinical.Title: Case 1
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 2-year-old male child is brought to the PHC by his mother. He has received vaccines only up to 14 weeks of age. Since then, no vaccination has been taken because the parents believed the child was "too old" for further vaccination. The child is otherwise healthy.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) What is your diagnosis?
2) What additional history will you obtain?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Partially immunized (defaulter) child needing catch-up immunization – there is no upper age limit under UIP; also ask reason for stopping, illness/AEFI history, caregiver beliefs, access barriers.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Prepare a catch-up immunization plan according to UIP.
2) Explain AEFI and post-vaccination advice.
3) Mention four counselling points for the parents.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Catch-up follows age-appropriate schedule with minimum intervals, no restart needed. AEFI = mild expected reactions (fever, local pain) vs serious AEFI needing reporting; advise antipyretic, 30-min post-vaccination observation. Counselling: no age cut-off for catch-up, vaccine safety, importance of completing schedule.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Using the WHO "Three C" model , construct a conceptual framework explaining this family's vaccine hesitancy and propose one intervention against each component.

clinical.Title: Case 2
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 9-month-old infant presents with loose stools for 2 days. The child is thirsty, has sunken eyes and skin pinch goes back slowly.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Classify the child's condition according to IMNCI.
2) Mention the clinical signs used to assess dehydration.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: IMNCI: Some dehydration. Signs: restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch goes back slowly.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Write the treatment plan with ORS and Zinc.
2) Mention danger signs requiring urgent referral.
3) Describe feeding and follow-up advice for the mother.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Plan B: ORS ~75ml/kg over 4 hours + Zinc (10-20mg/day x14 days). Danger signs: unable to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy. Advise continued feeding and follow-up in 5 days if not improving.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Evaluate the evidence base for low-osmolarity ORS and zinc in reducing diarrhoeal mortality, and comment on the reasons for poor coverage of ORS-Zinc despite programme availability.
clinical.Remarks: Case 2 – IMNCI: Diarrhoea with Some Dehydration

clinical.Title: Case 3
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 14-month-old child has profuse diarrhoea and vomiting for one day. The child is lethargic, unable to drink, radial pulse is feeble and skin pinch returns very slowly.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Classify this child's dehydration status.
2) Mention the clinical signs of severe dehydration seen here.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: IMNCI: Severe dehydration. Signs: lethargic/unconscious, unable to drink, very slow skin pinch, feeble pulse.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Describe IMNCI Plan C management including the IV fluid schedule.
2) Outline referral advice and pre-referral stabilization.
3) Suggest preventive measures against recurrence.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Plan C: IV Ringer's Lactate 100ml/kg (30ml/kg in 1st hour for <12 months, then 70ml/kg over 5 hours); if IV unavailable, refer urgently with NG-tube ORS en route. Prevention: safe water, hand hygiene, exclusive breastfeeding.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Critically analyse why children still die of dehydrating diarrhoea despite an effective, low-cost treatment, using the "three delays" framework .
clinical.Answer_Key_C: (delay in recognition, in reaching care, in receiving care)

clinical.Title: Case 4
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 10-month-old child presents with cough, fever and fast breathing. Respiratory rate is 62/min with lower chest indrawing.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Classify this child's condition according to IMNCI.
2) What general danger signs should be looked for?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: IMNCI: Severe pneumonia (RR ≥50/min for this age group with chest indrawing). Danger signs: unable to drink/breastfeed, convulsions, lethargic/unconscious, stridor in a calm child.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline treatment according to IMNCI for this classification.
2) Give home care advice to the mother.
3) Describe follow-up and criteria for reassessment.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Give first dose of antibiotic and refer urgently. Home care: continue feeding/fluids, keep warm. Follow-up: reassess in 2 days or immediately if worsening.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the role of PCV and Hib vaccination, and household air pollution reduction, in reducing childhood pneumonia burden in India. Comment on current coverage.

clinical.Title: Case 5
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks presents with BP 160/110 mmHg, pedal oedema and severe headache. Urine albumin is ++.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) What is your diagnosis?
2) Mention the high-risk factors for this condition.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Severe pre-eclampsia. Risk factors: primigravida, extremes of maternal age, obesity, chronic hypertension, family history, multiple pregnancy.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Describe immediate management at PHC, including the magnesium sulphate regimen.
2) State the indications and process for referral.
3) Counselling regarding danger signs and continued antenatal care.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: MgSO4 (Pritchard/loading + maintenance regimen) with antihypertensives, then refer to higher centre. Referral indicated for uncontrolled BP, imminent eclampsia, or facility limitations.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the role of quality antenatal care in early detection of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and critically comment on why maternal deaths from eclampsia persist despite the PMSMA and JSY programmes.

clinical.Title: Case 6
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 2-day-old newborn is being fed cow's milk through a bottle because the grandmother believes breast milk has "not yet come."
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the problem in this scenario.
2) Mention the disadvantages of top and bottle feeding.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Problem: prelacteal/delayed breastfeeding initiation due to a myth ("milk not yet come"). Disadvantages of top feeding: infection risk, allergy, nutritional inadequacy, loss of bonding/immunity.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Explain the advantages of early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding.
2) Demonstrate the counselling messages for the mother and grandmother.
3) Describe correct positioning and attachment.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Benefits: colostrum provides passive immunity, promotes bonding, reduces infection risk. Counselling should correct the myth and demonstrate correct positioning and attachment.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the influence of family and cultural beliefs on infant feeding practices, and outline how MAA (Mothers' Absolute Affection) and the IMS Act address these barriers.

clinical.Title: Case 7
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 55-year-old male with hypertension for 8 years comes for follow-up. BP is 170/104 mmHg despite irregular treatment. BMI is 31 kg/m² and he smokes.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Classify this patient's blood pressure.
2) Mention the modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors present.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Stage 2 hypertension (BP ≥160/100 mmHg). Modifiable: obesity, smoking, irregular treatment; non-modifiable: age.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline pharmacological management under NPCDCS/NP-NCD.
2) Give lifestyle modification advice.
3) Describe the follow-up and monitoring schedule.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Pharmacological: combination therapy (e.g., ACE inhibitor + calcium channel blocker). Lifestyle: weight loss, salt restriction, smoking cessation, exercise. Follow-up: monthly BP monitoring initially.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss population-based screening for hypertension under NP-NCD, and analyse the "rule of halves" as it applies to hypertension control in India.

clinical.Title: Case 8
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 52-year-old woman with diabetes for 10 years has FBS 220 mg/dL and HbA1c 9.5%. She has tingling in both feet.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) What is your diagnosis?
2) What complications should be screened for?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy. Screen for retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, cardiovascular risk, and diabetic foot.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline management at primary care level, including glycaemic targets.
2) Give lifestyle and foot-care counselling.
3) Describe follow-up investigations and referral criteria.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Management: lifestyle modification + metformin, target HbA1c <7%. Foot-care counselling: daily inspection, proper footwear. Follow-up: HbA1c every 3 months, renal function/lipids annually.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the concept of continuum of care for diabetes from Ayushman Arogya Mandir to district hospital, and comment on the role of the Health and Wellness Centre in NCD control.

clinical.Title: Case 9
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 15-year-old boy presents within one hour after a stray dog bite over the leg. His relatives applied turmeric and chilli powder over the wound.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Classify the category of exposure.
2) Describe immediate wound management, and comment on the application of turmeric and chilli.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Category III exposure (bleeding wound). Wound management: wash immediately with soap and running water for 15 minutes; turmeric/chilli application is harmful and should be discouraged as it can worsen the wound and delay proper care.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline the rabies post-exposure prophylaxis schedule per National Guidelines (route, site, schedule).
2) Explain the role and administration of Rabies Immunoglobulin.
3) Describe tetanus prophylaxis.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: PEP: intradermal/intramuscular anti-rabies vaccine schedule (e.g., Essen or updated Thai Red Cross regimen). RIG: infiltrate around the wound for Category III exposure. Tetanus prophylaxis per immunization status.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the One Health approach to rabies elimination in India, covering the National Rabies Control Programme, mass dog vaccination, and the 2030 elimination target.

clinical.Title: Case 10
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 45-year-old man has cough for one month, evening fever and weight loss. Sputum ZN stain is positive.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) What is your diagnosis?
2) What investigations would you order before starting treatment?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Pulmonary tuberculosis (NAAT positive). Investigations: rifampicin-resistance testing (CBNAAT), chest X-ray, HIV testing, baseline weight/LFT.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline the standard anti-TB regimen under NTEP with dosage and duration.
2) Give counselling regarding adherence and infection control.
3) Describe contact tracing and follow-up.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Regimen: 2HRZE/4HR daily FDC under NTEP. Counselling: adherence importance, cough hygiene/infection control. Contact tracing: screen household contacts, especially children <5 years.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Construct a conceptual framework linking social determinants (undernutrition, overcrowding, tobacco, delayed care-seeking) to TB transmission and outcomes, and map NTEP interventions onto it.

clinical.Title: Case 11
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 28 weeks of gestation attends the Antenatal Clinic for a routine check-up. She complains of easy fatigability, breathlessness on exertion and dizziness for the last one month. On examination: Pallor present; Pulse 96/min; BP 110/70 mmHg; mild bilateral pedal oedema; fundal height corresponds to 28 weeks; Hb = 8.2 g/dL; weight gain is inadequate; no active bleeding.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) What is the most likely diagnosis, and classify the severity per WHO?
2) What additional history and examination findings will you assess?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Moderate anaemia in pregnancy (WHO: Hb 7–9.9 g/dL). Additional history: dietary pattern, worm infestation, bleeding history; exam: pallor severity, oedema, cardiac signs.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline management per Anaemia Mukt Bharat/RMNCH guidelines.
2) Write six counselling messages for this woman.
3) Mention four maternal and four fetal complications of anaemia in pregnancy.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: AMB: oral iron-folic acid or IV iron sucrose depending on severity, dietary counselling. Complications: maternal (cardiac failure, PPH risk, infection); fetal (IUGR, preterm birth, low birth weight).
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Critically evaluate the Anaemia Mukt Bharat 6x6x6 strategy, and discuss why anaemia prevalence in pregnant women has not declined as expected in NFHS-5.

clinical.Title: Case 12
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 38-year-old male presents with multiple hypopigmented hypoesthetic skin patches over trunk and extensor surfaces, along with bilateral ulnar nerve thickening and claw hand deformity.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) What is the clinical classification according to WHO guidelines?
2) What clinical features support this classification?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Multibacillary (MB) leprosy – multiple lesions with nerve involvement (thickened ulnar nerve, claw hand).
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline the standard MDT regimen, dosage and duration.
2) Describe management of Type 1 and Type 2 lepra reactions.
3) Discuss deformity prevention and rehabilitation.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: MB-MDT: Rifampicin + Clofazimine + Dapsone for 12 months. Type 1 reaction: corticosteroids; Type 2 (ENL): steroids/clofazimine. Deformity prevention: self-care practices, protective footwear, physiotherapy.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss why new cases with Grade 2 disability continue to be detected despite elimination of leprosy as a public health problem, and outline the strategies under NLEP to address this.

clinical.Title: Case 13
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: An 18-month-old child is brought to PHC with severe wasting, MUAC = 10.5 cm, weight-for-height < -3 SD, bilateral pitting oedema, and loss of appetite.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Diagnose the nutritional condition and its severity.
2) State the NRC (Nutritional rehabilitation centre) admission criteria.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Severe Acute Malnutrition with bilateral pitting oedema (kwashiorkor-type SAM). NRC admission: SAM with medical complications, oedema, or failed appetite test.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline stabilization phase management with F-75.
2) Describe the catch-up growth phase with F-100 and discharge criteria.
3) Outline community-based management (CSAM) and follow-up.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Stabilization: F-75 (cautious, low-protein feeding). Catch-up: F-100 once appetite returns; discharge when oedema resolves and weight-for-height/MUAC criteria met. CSAM: home-based RUTF with growth monitoring follow-up.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the malnutrition–infection cycle in this child, and critically compare facility-based (NRC) versus community-based management of SAM in the Indian context.

clinical.Title: Case 14
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 32-year-old agricultural worker is brought to casualty in a confused state with miosis, excessive salivation, lacrimation, muscle fasciculations, and bradycardia following field spraying.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) State the clinical diagnosis.
2) List the clinical features / toxidrome of this case.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Organophosphate poisoning. Toxidrome: SLUDGE/DUMBBELS – salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI distress, emesis, miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhea, muscle fasciculations.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline emergency resuscitation and decontamination.
2) Describe the atropinization protocol and end-points.
3) Explain the role and dosing of Pralidoxime (PAM).
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Resuscitation: ABC, remove contaminated clothing, decontaminate skin. Atropinization: 2-4mg IV every 5-10 min until secretions dry/HR>80. PAM (Pralidoxime): 1-2g IV, most effective if given early.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss pesticide poisoning as an occupational and public health problem in India, covering means restriction, the role of the Insecticides Act, and preventive strategies for agricultural workers.

clinical.Title: Case 15
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 28-year-old male from a forest endemic zone presents with high-grade fever with chills, altered sensorium, jaundice, and urine output < 400 ml/24 hours. Peripheral smear shows P. falciparum ring forms.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) State the diagnosis
2) List the indicators  present in this patient.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Severe malaria (jaundice, altered sensorium, oliguria are severe indicators, along with hyperparasitaemia, acidosis, etc.).
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Write the parenteral Artesunate regimen and dosage.
2) Describe supportive management of jaundice, oliguria and altered sensorium.
3) Outline monitoring and criteria for switching to oral therapy.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: IV Artesunate 2.4mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours then once daily. Supportive care for fluid balance, renal/hepatic monitoring. Switch to oral ACT after ≥24h once able to tolerate orally and improving.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss vector control interventions under NVBDCP, and evaluate the challenges to the National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2030 in forest and tribal areas.

clinical.Title: Case 16
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 14-year-old schoolgirl presents at Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) clinic with fatigue, poor academic performance, and pallor. Hb is 9.5 g/dL.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Diagnose and clasify its severity
2) List the six thematic areas of RKSK.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Moderate anaemia (Hb 9.5 g/dL). RKSK 6 thematic areas: nutrition; sexual and reproductive health; non-communicable diseases; substance misuse; injuries and violence; mental health.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline the WIFS protocol and deworming schedule.
2) Describe the role of Saathiya peer educators.
3) Discuss the menstrual hygiene scheme and its school-level implementation.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: WIFS: weekly iron-folic acid tablet + biannual albendazole deworming. Saathiya: peer educators for adolescent health awareness. Menstrual hygiene scheme: sanitary napkin distribution with awareness sessions.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the determinants of adolescent anaemia in girls, and critically evaluate the effectiveness of school-based WIFS in improving haemoglobin levels.

clinical.Title: Case 17
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 62-year-old hypertensive and diabetic male presents with sudden-onset right-sided facial arm weakness and slurred speech within 2 hours of onset.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Recognize the stroke using FAST criteria.
2) What immediate stabilization would you provide at PHC?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Stabilization: ABC, check blood glucose, keep nil by mouth, urgent transport.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Outline the referral pathway to district hospital and the significance of the thrombolysis window.
2) Describe secondary prevention strategies under NP-NCD.
3) Outline long-term rehabilitation and risk-factor control.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Referral: thrombolysis window is typically within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Secondary prevention: antiplatelets, statins, BP/glycaemic control. Rehab: physiotherapy and risk-factor modification.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss stroke as an emerging public health problem in India, covering the epidemiological transition, pre-hospital delay, and organisation of stroke care services.

clinical.Title: Case 18
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 70-year-old female living alone visits Ayushman Arogya Mandir with osteoarthritis knee, visual impairment, and feeling neglected.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Enumerate components of comprehensive geriatric assessment at primary care.
2) Identify the specific problems present in this patient.
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Components: functional, cognitive, nutritional, and social assessment; vision/hearing screening; polypharmacy review. Problems present: osteoarthritis, visual impairment, social isolation/neglect.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Detail services provided under NPHCE.
2) Outline assistive devices and social security pension linkages.
3) Describe the domiciliary visit protocol.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: NPHCE services: geriatric OPD/ward at district level, physiotherapy, assistive devices. Assistive devices: walking aids, spectacles; pension: old-age pension schemes. Domiciliary visits: periodic home visits by health worker.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss population ageing in India and its health system implications, and outline strategies to address social isolation and elder neglect at the community level.

clinical.Title: Case 19
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 25-year-old farmer presents with fever of 8 days, black eschar over groin, generalized lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the rickettsial disease and its vector.
2) What is the diagnostic significance of the eschar, and what confirmatory tests would you order?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Scrub typhus; vector: trombiculid mite (chigger). Eschar is pathognomonic; confirmatory tests: Weil-Felix test, IgM ELISA.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Write the drug of choice, dosage and duration.
2) What complications should be monitored for?
3) Describe vector control and personal protective measures in rural settings.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Doxycycline 100mg BD for 7-10 days. Complications: ARDS, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis, multi-organ dysfunction. Vector control: scrub clearance, DEET repellent, protective clothing.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the approach to a case of acute undifferentiated febrile illness in a rural Indian setting, and the public health importance of scrub typhus as a re-emerging infection.

clinical.Title: Case 20
clinical.Scenario_or_Stem: A 42-year-old stone crusher worker presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, and chest X-ray showing egg-shell calcification of hilar lymph nodes.
clinical.Sub_Question_A:
1) Diagnose this case and identify the causative exposure.
2) What finding supports this diagnosis?
clinical.Answer_Key_A: Silicosis; causative exposure: crystalline silica dust. Radiological finding: egg-shell calcification of hilar lymph nodes.
clinical.Sub_Question_B:
1) Explain preventive measures under the Factories Act.
2) Describe the statutory notification and compensation procedure.
3) Explain the formal procedures and long‑term support systems available for this diseases.
clinical.Answer_Key_B: Prevention: wet drilling, local exhaust ventilation, N95 respirators. Notification: statutory notifiable occupational disease, compensation under relevant labour law. Silicosis Board: state-level registration, compensation, and rehabilitation.
clinical.Sub_Question_C: Construct a conceptual framework of the occupational exposure pathway from silica dust to permanent disability, identifying preventive intervention points at the level of the worker, the workplace, and legislation.

epidemiology.Title: EPIDEMIOLOGY EXAMINATION
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Instructions: Answer all sub-questions carefully.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 1
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: In a town with mid-year population of 150,000: Total live births = 3,200; Total deaths = 1,400; Infant deaths = 270; Maternal deaths = 10.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Calculate the Crude Birth Rate (CBR).
2) Calculate the Crude Death Rate (CDR).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR).
2) Calculate the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR).
3) Compare these rates against national/state averages.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: IMR = (270/3,200) × 1,000 = 84.4 per 1,000 live births. MMR = (10/3,200) × 100,000 = 312.5 per 100,000 live births. Both IMR and MMR are considerably higher than current national averages (India IMR ~28, MMR ~97).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret all four calculated rates together and identify which indicate a public health concern.
2) Suggest maternal and child health interventions this town should prioritize.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C: IMR and MMR indicate a significant public health concern; CBR/CDR are within plausible range. Priorities: strengthen antenatal/intranatal/postnatal care, skilled birth attendance, referral transport, and newborn care services.
epidemiology.Remarks: In a town with mid-year population of 150,000

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 2
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Town population 50,000. TB cases and deaths by sex: Male – 400 TB cases, 150 deaths, population 24,000; Female – 600 TB cases, 200 deaths, population 26,000; Total – 1,000 TB cases, 350 deaths, population 50,000.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Calculate the crude death rate.
2) Calculate the sex-specific death rate (male and female).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the prevalence of TB.
2) Calculate the case fatality rate.
3) Comment on which sub-group needs closer surveillance.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret all four calculated indicators together.
2) Discuss surveillance and referral measures to reduce TB case fatality.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C: All four indicators point to a high TB burden and unusually high case fatality (35%) for TB, suggesting delayed diagnosis/treatment failure. Females show a higher death rate and need closer surveillance. Strengthen active case finding, DOTS adherence, and nutritional support.
epidemiology.Remarks: From the given data of a town for the year 2014

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 3
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Researchers recruited two groups of adults based on their lipid profile status and followed them over the next several years to observe development of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Among 200 individuals with a high lipid profile, 30 developed CVD during follow-up. Among 500 individuals with a normal lipid profile, 50 developed CVD during follow-up.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the study design used here.
2) Calculate the incidence of CVD in both groups.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Cohort study (prospective). Incidence: high lipid group = 15/115 = 13.0%; normal lipid group = 85/985 = 8.6%.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the test of association.
3) Comment on the strength of association shown.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Relative Risk = 13.0%/8.6% ≈ 1.51. Attributable Risk Proportion (in exposed) = (13.0-8.6)/13.0 ≈ 33.8%.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret both measures together in terms of excess CVD burden attributable to abnormal lipid profile.
2) Discuss community-level primary prevention strategies for dyslipidemia.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C: About 34% of CVD among the high-lipid group is attributable to abnormal lipid profile itself; a moderate excess risk. This supports targeted lipid screening and statin/lifestyle intervention in high-risk individuals.
epidemiology.Remarks: Data from cohort study on blood lipid profile and cardiovascular disease

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 4
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Investigators identified persons who sustained a head injury following a road traffic accident as one group, and persons who did not sustain a head injury as another group, then traced back their helmet-use status at the time of the accident. Among 500 persons with head injury, 200 had not used a helmet and 300 had used a helmet. Among 500 persons without head injury, 50 had not used a helmet and 450 had used a helmet.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the study design used here.
2) Calculate the test of association.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Case-control study. Odds Ratio = (200×450)/(50×300) = 90,000/15,000 = 6.0.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Interpret the results.
2) State whether helmet use is protective or a risk factor.
3) Mention advantages and disadvantages of this design.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: OR = 6 means persons without a helmet had 6 times the odds of head injury compared to helmet users — helmet use is protective (absence of helmet is a risk factor).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Discuss road safety measures relevant to this finding.
2) Discuss helmet-enforcement and legislative measures.
epidemiology.Remarks: Data from study on helmet use and head injury following RTA

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 5
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Outbreak of acute gastroenteritis during a birthday party attended by 50 persons, of whom 10 became ill. Food-specific exposures: Ice-creams – 40 ate, 4 cases; Chicken curry – 20 ate, 10 cases; Butter Paneer – 35 ate, 7 cases.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the type of study design used in this outbreak investigation.
2) Calculate the overall attack rate.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Retrospective cohort (outbreak investigation). Overall attack rate = 10/50 = 20%.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the food-specific attack rates.
2) Identify the likely vehicle of transmission and justify your choice.
3) Compare overall vs food-specific attack rates.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Food-specific attack rates: Ice-cream = 4/40 = 10%; Chicken curry = 10/20 = 50%; Butter Paneer = 7/35 = 20%. Chicken curry has the highest attack rate among exposed — most likely vehicle of transmission.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret the attack rate data together to confirm the source.
2) Outline the outbreak investigation and control measures you would recommend.
epidemiology.Remarks: The following data of an outbreak of acute gastroenteritis during birthday party

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 6
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Investigators identified women diagnosed with cervical cancer as one group, and women without cervical cancer as another group, then obtained their HPV vaccination history. Among 500 women with cervical cancer, 200 were not immunized and 300 were immunized. Among 500 women without cervical cancer, 50 were not immunized and 450 were immunized.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the study design used here.
2) Calculate the measure of association.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Case-control study. Odds Ratio = (200×450)/(300×50) = 90,000/15,000 = 6.0.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Interpret the measure of association.
2) State its implication for HPV vaccination as a preventive strategy.
3) Mention advantages and disadvantages of this design.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: OR = 6 means unimmunized women had 6 times the odds of cervical cancer compared to immunized women — supports HPV vaccination as a strongly protective intervention.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Discuss the national HPV vaccination programme.
2) Discuss cervical cancer screening strategy relevant here.
epidemiology.Remarks: Data from case control study on HPV vaccination & cervical cancer

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 7
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: A rapid diagnostic test for pulmonary tuberculosis is compared with the gold standard confirmatory test: Test positive – disease present 800, disease absent 1,000; Test negative – disease present 200, disease absent 8,000.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the type of study design used to evaluate this test and make the 2*2 table.
2) Calculate sensitivity.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Diagnostic accuracy (cross-sectional) study. Sensitivity = 800/(800+200) = 80%.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate specificity.
2) Calculate PPV.
3) Calculate NPV.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret all four calculated measures together and comment on the test's suitability for TB screening in the field.
2) Explain the concept of parallel and series (serial) testing, and discuss which approach would be more appropriate when combining this rapid test with the gold standard test.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C: Low PPV (44%) reflects low prevalence in this sample; high NPV makes the test good for ruling out TB but positive results need gold-standard confirmation — suited as a triage/screening tool, not a stand-alone diagnostic test.
epidemiology.Remarks: Results of a Rapid diagnostic test for pulmonary tuberculosis compared with gold standard

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 8
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: In a community of 4,000 persons, 120 became ill with a disease of unknown etiology, occurring in 75 households with a total of 475 persons; one primary case per household.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the type of study design used in this investigation.
2) Calculate the overall attack rate.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Outbreak investigation (retrospective cohort). Overall attack rate = 120/4,000 = 3%.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the secondary attack rate.
2) Comment on the extent of person-to-person spread.
3) Compare overall and secondary attack rate values.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Secondary attack rate = (Total cases − primary cases)/(Total household contacts − primary cases) = (120−75)/(475−75) = 45/400 = 11.25%.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret both attack rates together regarding transmission dynamics.
2) Recommend outbreak containment measures for this setting.
epidemiology.Remarks: In a particular community, 120 persons in a population of 4,000 became ill

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 9
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: A new diagnostic test for cancer is compared with the complete diagnostic package in current use: Test positive – disease present 8, disease absent 1,000; Test negative – disease present 2, disease absent 9,000.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the type of study design used to evaluate this test and make the 2*2 table.
2) Calculate sensitivity.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Diagnostic accuracy study. Sensitivity = 8/10 = 80%.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate specificity.
2) Calculate PPV.
3) Calculate NPV.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) what will be the new PPV and NPV if prevalence increased by 10%.
2) Discuss implications of false positives/negatives for this screening programme.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C: Very low PPV due to low disease prevalence — most positives will be false positives in population-level screening; NPV near 100% makes it excellent for ruling the disease out.
epidemiology.Remarks: Results of a new diagnostic test for cancer compared with gold standard

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 10
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: PHC area population 30,000, with 5,200 women of reproductive age (15–44 years) reporting 840 live births in 1 year.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Calculate the General Fertility Rate (GFR).
2) Calculate the Crude Birth Rate (CBR).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Compare the GFR and CBR values obtained.
2) Explain why GFR is more valid than CBR.
3) Discuss demographic significance of the reproductive-age population here.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: GFR is a more valid fertility indicator than CBR because its denominator (women of reproductive age) is the population actually at risk of childbearing, whereas CBR's denominator includes men, children, and elderly who cannot give birth.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret both rates together and their combined implication for this population's fertility status.
2) Suggest a more refined indicator (ASFR/TFR) for this population.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 11
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Data: Live births = 4,500; Stillbirths (>1000g) = 44; Deaths < 7 days = 100; Deaths 7–28 days = 75; Deaths 28 days to 1 year = 165.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Calculate the Early Neonatal Mortality Rate.
2) Calculate the Late Neonatal Mortality Rate.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Early Neonatal Mortality Rate = (100/4,500) × 1,000 = 22.2 per 1,000 live births. Late Neonatal Mortality Rate = (75/4,500) × 1,000 = 16.7 per 1,000 live births.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the Perinatal Mortality Rate.
2) Calculate the Post-Neonatal Mortality Rate.
3) Calculate the Infant Mortality Rate.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Perinatal Mortality Rate = (44+100)/(4,500+44) × 1,000 = 31.7 per 1,000 total births. Post-Neonatal Mortality Rate = (165/4,500) × 1,000 = 36.7 per 1,000 live births. Infant Mortality Rate = (100+75+165)/4,500 × 1,000 = 75.6 per 1,000 live births.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret all five calculated rates together, noting the relative contribution of neonatal vs post-neonatal deaths.
2) Suggest interventions to reduce perinatal mortality based on these findings.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C: Post-neonatal deaths (36.7) contribute more than neonatal deaths (22.2+16.7=38.9 combined, roughly comparable) — both periods need attention: perinatal/neonatal care for early deaths and infection/nutrition control for post-neonatal deaths.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 12
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Under-5 deaths vs total deaths: India (Total deaths = 500, U5 deaths = 156); USA (Total deaths = 80, U5 deaths = 4); Japan (Total deaths = 50, U5 deaths = 1).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Calculate the Proportional Mortality Rate for under-5s in India.
2) Calculate it for USA and Japan.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Compare health development status using PMR.
2) Rank the countries by child health status.
3) Explain why under-5 PMR reflects environmental health status.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret all three calculated PMR values together, explaining the pattern.
2) Discuss factors behind the gap between India and Japan, and suggest measures.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C: India's much higher proportional under-5 mortality reflects poorer environmental sanitation, nutrition, and health service access compared to USA/Japan; the gap highlights the need for continued MCH programme investment.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 13
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: 1,000 hypertensive patients were randomly allocated to receive a new antihypertensive drug, and another 1,000 comparable hypertensive patients were randomly allocated to receive a placebo; both groups were followed for the same period. Among those receiving the drug, 20 developed stroke. Among those receiving the placebo, 50 developed stroke.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the study design used here.
2) Calculate the Experimental Event Rate (EER).
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). EER = 20/1,000 = 2%.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the Control Event Rate (CER).
2) Calculate the Absolute Risk Reduction.
3) Calculate the Relative Risk Reduction.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Calculate the Number Needed to Treat, and interpret all calculated measures together in terms of clinical efficacy.
2) Discuss the clinical usefulness of this drug for stroke prevention.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C: NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.03 ≈ 34 (need to treat ~34 patients to prevent one stroke). Despite a large relative benefit (60% RRR), the absolute benefit is modest — clinically useful but should be weighed against cost and side effects.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 14
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Cholera outbreak in a village: Curve showing number of cases within 36 hours.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the type of epidemic curve shown.
2) List characteristic features.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Point-source (single exposure) epidemic curve. Features: rapid, sharp rise; all cases clustered within one incubation period; symmetric/steep decline; no secondary wave.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Estimate the probable time of exposure using median incubation period.
2) Explain the reasoning used to calculate exposure time.
3) Comment on what the plot indicates about the source.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Estimate: probable exposure time = time of the peak minus the median incubation period for the suspected agent (e.g., for cholera, ~1–3 days incubation — subtract from peak time).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Outline immediate outbreak containment measures for this village.
2) Discuss measures to prevent future  cholera outbreaks.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 15
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Industrial plant workers (n=5,000): Observed deaths = 45; Expected deaths based on general population age-specific mortality rates = 30.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the study design used here.
2) Calculate the Standardized Mortality Ratio.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Retrospective occupational cohort study. SMR = (45/30) × 100 = 150.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Interpret whether mortality is significantly elevated.
2) Discuss possible occupational reasons for elevated mortality.
3) Comment on the "healthy worker effect" and its relevance here.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: SMR of 150 indicates 50% excess mortality compared to the general population — statistically and occupationally significant, warranting investigation of workplace hazards.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Distinguish between Direct and Indirect Standardization.
2) Discuss when Indirect Standardization is preferred over Direct.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 16
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: A survey was conducted among 1,000 adults, recording their current physical activity level and body weight status at a single point in time. Among 400 adults with a sedentary lifestyle, 120 were found to be obese and 280 were not. Among 600 adults with an active lifestyle, 60 were found to be obese and 540 were not.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the study design used here.
2) Calculate the Prevalence Odds Ratio.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Study design: Cross-sectional study. Prevalence Odds Ratio = (120×540)/(280×60) = 64,800/16,800 ≈ 3.86.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the Prevalence Ratio.
2) Compare the POR and PR values.
3) Explain why POR overestimates PR when outcome prevalence is high.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Prevalence Ratio = (120/400)/(60/600) = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0. POR (3.86) overestimates PR (3.0) because obesity prevalence is high (>10%) in both groups — the rare-disease assumption behind OR≈RR breaks down.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret both measures together regarding the sedentary-obesity association.
2) Explain why causal inference cannot be established in this design.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 17
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Study on Coffee drinking and Bladder Cancer: Crude OR = 2.5; Stratified by Smoking Status: Stratum 1 (Smokers OR = 1.0), Stratum 2 (Non-smokers OR = 1.0).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify the study design suggested by the use of odds ratio as the measure of association.
2) Identify whether smoking is a confounder or effect modifier here.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A:
Case control
Smoking is a confounder here, not an effect modifier — the stratum-specific ORs (both 1.0) are similar to each other but very different from the crude OR (2.5).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Justify your answer using the crude and stratum-specific ORs given.
2) Explain methods to control confounding at the design stage.
3) Explain methods to control confounding at the analysis stage.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Since stratifying by smoking removes the association (crude OR 2.5 → stratum ORs both 1.0), smoking meets the criteria for a classic confounder rather than an effect modifier (which would show different ORs between strata).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) State the criteria for a variable to be defined as a confounder.
2) Distinguish confounding from effect modification using this example.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 18
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: In an emerging respiratory virus outbreak, mean serial interval is 5 days and index case infects an average of 2.8 secondary cases in susceptible population.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Define the Basic Reproduction Number (R0).
2) Define Serial Interval.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: R0 (Basic Reproduction Number) = average number of secondary cases generated by one infectious case in a fully susceptible population ≈ 2.8 here. Serial Interval = time between symptom onset in a primary case and symptom onset in a secondary case ≈ 5 days here.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the Critical Vaccination Coverage (Vc) required for herd immunity.
2) Explain the formula used and its assumptions.
3) Discuss the relationship between R0 and speed of spread here.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Vc = 1 − 1/R0 = 1 − 1/2.8 ≈ 0.643, i.e., about 64.3% of the population needs to be immune to achieve herd immunity.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret the public health significance of Rt falling below 1.
2) Discuss measures that could help bring Rt below 1 in this outbreak.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 19
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: A District Health Officer evaluates AFP (Acute Flaccid Paralysis) and Fever-Rash surveillance reporting from primary health centres.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Distinguish between Active, Passive, and Sentinel Surveillance with examples.
2) Identify which type is used for AFP reporting under Polio Eradication.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: Active surveillance: health workers actively seek out cases (e.g., house-to-house AFP case search). Passive surveillance: facilities report cases as part of routine reporting. Sentinel surveillance: selected representative sites report data. AFP surveillance under Polio Eradication uses active surveillance.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) List key indicators for evaluating AFP surveillance performance.
2) Explain the significance of the non-polio AFP rate as a quality indicator.
3) Discuss the role of fever-rash surveillance in measles-rubella elimination.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Key AFP indicators: Non-Polio AFP rate (target ≥2/100,000 children <15 years), stool adequacy rate (≥80% with 2 samples 24h apart within 14 days of onset), timeliness of reporting.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Define IDSP and its objectives.
2) Differentiate syndromic, presumptive, and confirmed case reporting under IDSP.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 20
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: Life Table parameters: lx = 100,000 live births; dx = deaths between age x and x+n; ex = expectation of life at age x.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Define expectation of life at birth (e0).
2) Explain how infant mortality impacts e0.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_A: e0 = the average number of years a newborn is expected to live if current age-specific mortality rates remain constant throughout its life.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) List major uses of complete life tables in public health planning.
2) Explain how life tables inform DALYs and Healthy Life Expectancy.
3) Discuss how lx and dx help project population survival.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_B: Higher infant mortality substantially lowers e0 because deaths in the very first year of life remove many potential years of life from the population average.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Differentiate between Abridged and Complete Life Tables.
2) Discuss when an Abridged Life Table would be preferred.

epidemiology.Title: Epidemiology - 21
epidemiology.Scenario_or_Stem: A PHC area has a population of 1,00,000. During the year, 10,000 blood smears were examined for malaria. Of these, 500 slides were positive, and 200 of the positive slides showed P. falciparum.
epidemiology.Sub_Question_A:
1) Calculate the Annual Blood Examination Rate (ABER).
2) Calculate the Slide Positivity Rate (SPR).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_B:
1) Calculate the Annual Parasite Incidence (API).
2) Calculate the Slide Falciparum Rate (SFR).
3) Calculate the Annual Falciparum Incidence (AfPI).
epidemiology.Sub_Question_C:
1) Interpret all five indicators together and comment on the malaria endemicity and transmission intensity in this PHC area.
2) Discuss the programmatic significance of ABER as a surveillance quality indicator under NVBDCP, and the actions triggered by a high API.
epidemiology.Answer_Key_C:
Interpretation: ABER 10% shows adequate surveillance, SPR 5% indicates moderate transmission, API 5/1000 suggests meso-endemic malaria, SFR 40% highlights significant falciparum burden, AfPI 2/1000 confirms notable falciparum transmission. 
Programmatic significance: ABER reflects surveillance quality under NVBDCP, while high API (>2/1000) triggers intensified control measures like active case detection, vector control, and strengthened community interventions.

biostatistics.Title: BIOSTATISTICS EXAMINATION
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Instructions: Answer all sub-questions carefully.
biostatistics.Remarks: Section Header

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 1
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: In a school health check-up, haemoglobin level was estimated in 300 children.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Calculate the mean haemoglobin level of the school children.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: Calculate the standard deviation and comment on the variability of haemoglobin levels in this population.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the public health significance of these haemoglobin levels for anaemia control in school children.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a histogram with frequency polygon on graph paper.
biostatistics.Remarks: In a school health check-up, haemoglobin level was estimated in 300 children
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: SD ≈ 1.69 g% (variance = Σf(x-mean)²/N = 852/300 = 2.84). Moderate variability; a sizeable proportion of children fall in the lower Hb range, indicating anaemia burden.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 2
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Respiratory rate of 10 asthma patients: 18, 20, 19, 20, 18, 19, 16, 25, 23, 17.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Calculate the mean, mean deviation, and standard deviation.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: Interpret the coefficient of variation for this dataset and comment on the spread of respiratory rate values.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the clinical significance of variability in respiratory rate monitoring in asthma patients.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Draw a box-and-whisker plot marking median, Q1, Q3, and outliers.
biostatistics.Remarks: Respiratory rate of 10 asthma patients
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Mean = 19.5 breaths/min. Mean Deviation = 2.05. Standard Deviation ≈ 2.72 (sample, n-1).
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: CV = (2.72/19.5)×100 ≈ 13.9% — moderate relative variability, expected given individual variation in asthma severity.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 3
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Pulse rate per minute of 12 normal individuals: 59, 62, 64, 65, 68, 73, 74, 75, 78, 80, 80, 86.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Calculate the mean, mean deviation, SD, coefficient of variation, and range.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: Compare the coefficient of variation with the standard deviation and state which better describes relative variability.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the normal physiological range of pulse rate and the significance of any outliers in this dataset.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Draw a box-and-whisker plot marking median, Q1, Q3, and outliers.
biostatistics.Remarks: Pulse rate per minute of 12 normal individuals
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Mean = 72/min. Mean Deviation = 7. SD ≈ 8.38 (sample, n-1). CV ≈ 11.6%. Range = 86−59 = 27.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: CV (11.6%) and SD (8.38) both indicate moderate variability; CV is more useful for comparing relative variability across datasets with different units/means.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 4
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Out of 250 diarrhoeal cases with dehydration, 150 were treated with homemade fluid and 100 with ORS.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Test the difference in outcome between ORS and homemade fluid.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the appropriate test of significance for comparing these two proportions and the assumptions it requires.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the public health implications for promoting ORS use over homemade fluids in diarrhoea management.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a component (stacked) bar chart showing the proportion recovered in the ORS and homemade fluid groups.
biostatistics.Remarks: Out of 250 diarrheal cases with dehydration, 150 treated with homemade fluid, 100 with ORS
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Recovered: Homemade fluid 120/150 = 80%; ORS 70/100 = 70%. Chi-square test ≈ 3.29 (df=1); not significant at 5% (critical value 3.84, p>0.05) in this sample.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Chi-square test for two proportions; assumes independent observations, expected cell counts ≥5 (met here), and a 2×2 contingency table.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 5
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: The distribution of eye colour by sex of 500 American children is given.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Test the association between eye colour and sex.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State which test of significance is appropriate for this categorical data and why.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Comment on whether eye colour and sex are likely to be biologically associated, and the limitations of applying statistical tests here.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a grouped (dodged) bar chart showing eye colour distribution separately for males and females.
biostatistics.Remarks: Distribution of eye color by sex of 500 American children
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Chi-square test for association ≈ 3.97 (df=1); significant at 5% (critical value 3.84, p<0.05) in this sample.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Chi-square test of independence is appropriate for two categorical variables (eye colour, sex) in a contingency table.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 6
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Systolic BP was measured in 10 patients before and after a 6-week yoga intervention.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Calculate the mean difference and standard deviation of the differences.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: Apply the paired t-test and state whether the reduction in BP is statistically significant.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the clinical significance of this BP reduction and its implications for non-pharmacological management of hypertension.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a paired dot plot (before–after plot) connecting each patient's pre- and post-intervention BP.
biostatistics.Remarks: A screening test (PAP smear) was done for cervical cancer
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Mean difference = 12.2 mmHg. SD of differences ≈ 1.23 mmHg.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Paired t = 12.2/(1.23/√10) ≈ 31.4, df=9; far exceeds the critical t-value (~2.26 at 5%) — statistically highly significant reduction in BP (p<0.001).

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 7
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: A primary health centre covering 30,000 population has a crude birth rate of 25/1,000 mid-year population and infant mortality rate of 70/1,000 live births.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Estimate the vaccine requirement for the birth cohort for a 1-year period and outline how you would organize the routine immunization programme.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: Calculate the expected number of infant deaths per year and comment on whether the IMR indicates a public health priority.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss immunization programme planning (cold chain, staffing, wastage factor) needed to meet the estimated vaccine requirement.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a component bar chart showing the vaccine dose requirement (net requirement plus wastage) for each UIP antigen.
biostatistics.Remarks: A PHC covering 30,000 population has CBR 25/1000, IMR 70/1000
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Expected infant deaths = 750×(70/1,000) ≈ 53/year. An IMR of 70/1,000 is well above the current national average (~28/1,000), indicating this is a public health priority area.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 8
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: In a study of 130 individuals
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Apply and interpret a test of significance at 95% CI.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the null hypothesis being tested and the appropriate statistical test for this 2×2 comparison.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss counselling points for OCP use in women with risk factors for hypertension.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a component (stacked) bar chart showing the proportion of hypertensive individuals among OCP users and non-users.
biostatistics.Remarks: In a study, out of 60 hypertensives, 30 used OCP; among 70 non-hypertensives, 25 used OCP
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: OR of 1.8 indicates a weak-to-moderate positive association — OCP users have about 1.8 times the odds of hypertension compared to non-users; clinically relevant enough to warrant BP monitoring.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 9
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: The outcome of DOTS therapy in 200 patients (110 male, 90 female) is given.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Apply and interpret a test of significance at 95% CI.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the null hypothesis being tested and the appropriate statistical test for this 2×2 comparison.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss programmatic implications if treatment outcomes differ significantly between sexes under DOTS.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a component (stacked) bar chart showing cure rate (%) by sex.
biostatistics.Remarks: Outcome of DOTS therapy in males and females
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Chi-square ≈ 3.96 (df=1); significant at 5% (critical value 3.84, p<0.05). Cure rate: male 83/110=75.5%, female 78/90=86.7%.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Null hypothesis: cure rate is independent of sex. Chi-square test for association in a 2×2 table is appropriate.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 10
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: A drug trial recorded heart rate increase in treated and untreated groups.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Apply and interpret a test of significance at 95% CI.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the null and alternative hypotheses for this trial and the test statistic used.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the clinical significance of the result versus its statistical significance.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a component (stacked) bar chart showing the proportion with increased heart rate in each group.
biostatistics.Remarks: A drug trial showed following results
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Chi-square ≈ 3.42 (df=1); not significant at 5% (critical value 3.84, p>0.05) — borderline result.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Null hypothesis: no difference in heart-rate-increase proportion between treated and untreated groups. Alternative: a difference exists. Chi-square test statistic used.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 11
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: A mortality study compared survival outcomes in diseased and non-diseased persons .
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Apply and interpret a test of significance at 95% CI.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the appropriate test of significance for comparing these mortality figures and its underlying assumptions.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the public health implications if the difference in mortality is found to be statistically significant.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a component (stacked) bar chart showing the proportion died/survived by disease status.
biostatistics.Remarks: A mortality study showed following data
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Chi-square ≈ 7.78 (df=1); significant at 1% (p<0.01). Mortality: diseased 10/35=28.6%, not diseased 5/65=7.7% (RR≈3.7).
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Chi-square test of significance for two proportions; assumes independent observations and adequate expected cell counts (met here).

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 12
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Data on smoking and presence of lung cancer is given.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Apply and interpret a test of significance at 95% CI.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: Calculate the odds ratio from this data and interpret the strength of association between smoking and lung cancer.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss tobacco control measures relevant to reducing this risk at the population level.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a component (stacked) bar chart showing the proportion with lung cancer among smokers and non-smokers.
biostatistics.Remarks: Data on smoking and presence of lung cancer
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: OR of 4.8 indicates a strong positive association — smokers have nearly 5 times the odds of lung cancer compared to non-smokers.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 13
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Birth weights were observed in two groups of infants, Group A and Group B.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Test and interpret whether the mean birth weights differ significantly.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the appropriate test for comparing these two means and the assumption of normality involved.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the maternal and child health implications if the mean birth weights differ significantly between groups.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a box-and-whisker plot comparing birth weight distribution in Group A and Group B.
biostatistics.Remarks: Birth weights in 2 groups of infants
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: t ≈ 2.30; with large sample size, approximately significant at 5% (critical ≈1.96) — Group B's mean birth weight is significantly higher.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Independent (unpaired) two-sample t-test (or Z-test given large n); assumes approximately normal distribution of birth weights in each group and independent samples.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 14
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Random blood sugar (RBS) samples were taken from two populations, A and B.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Apply and interpret a test of significance at 95% CI.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the appropriate test of significance for comparing these two means and its assumptions.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the public health implications of a significant difference in random blood sugar between the two populations.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a box-and-whisker plot comparing RBS distribution in Population A and Population B.
biostatistics.Remarks: RBS sample from 2 populations
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Z ≈ 17.3; highly significant (p<0.001) — Population B has a significantly higher mean RBS than Population A.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Z-test for comparing two independent means (large sample sizes); assumes approximately normal distribution and independent samples.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 15
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: A cross-sectional study recorded weekly oil intake per household in Town X and Town Y.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Apply and interpret a test of significance at 95% CI.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the appropriate test for comparing oil intake between the groups and its underlying assumptions.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss dietary counselling measures relevant to reducing excess oil/fat intake in the community.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a box-and-whisker plot comparing oil intake distribution in Town X and Town Y.
biostatistics.Remarks: A cross-sectional study showed oil intake per week
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Z ≈ 2.66; significant at 5% (p<0.01) — Town X has significantly higher oil intake than Town Y.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Z-test for comparing two independent means (large sample sizes); assumes independent random samples and approximately normal distribution of intake.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 16
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: The results of a study of association between contraceptive type and hypertension are given.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Test and interpret whether the proportions differ significantly.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the appropriate test for comparing these two proportions and the conditions required for its validity.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss counselling and monitoring measures for hypertension risk in women using contraceptives.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a component (stacked) bar chart showing the proportion hypertensive among oral vs other contraceptive users.
biostatistics.Remarks: Study of contraceptives and hypertension
biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Z ≈ 0.58; not significant (p>0.05) — no statistically significant difference in hypertension prevalence between contraceptive types in this sample.
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Z-test for comparing two independent proportions; requires adequately large sample sizes and independent groups (both satisfied here).

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 17
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Data collected from a diabetic clinic on prevalence by sex is given.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Test and interpret whether the proportions differ significantly.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the appropriate test of significance for comparing these proportions and interpret the result.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the implications for diabetes care/monitoring protocols at the clinic based on this finding.
biostatistics.Plot_Instruction: Construct a grouped (dodged) bar chart comparing diabetes prevalence (%) between males and females.
biostatistics.Remarks: Data collected from diabetic clinic

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 18
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: The incidence of myocardial infarction (MI) by sex is given.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_A: Test and interpret whether the proportions differ significantly.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_B: State the appropriate test of significance for comparing these incidence proportions and interpret the result.
biostatistics.Sub_Question_C: Discuss cardiovascular risk-reduction measures relevant to the population with higher incidence.

biostatistics.Answer_Key_A: Z ≈ 2.39; significant at 5% (p<0.05) — male MI incidence (42%) is significantly higher than female (38%).
biostatistics.Answer_Key_B: Z-test for two independent proportions; both groups are large, satisfying the normal approximation.

biostatistics.Title: Biostatistics - 19
biostatistics.Scenario_or_Stem: Bivariate dataset of Body Mass Index (BMI) and Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) in 15 patients: r = +0.78, p < 0.01.

ospe.Title: OSPE EXAMINATION
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: Instructions: Answer all sub-questions carefully.

ospe.Title: Station 1
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: 54-year-old male with type 2 diabetes, tingling/numbness in feet.
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) Components of inspection
2) Peripheral pulses
3) Neuropathy assessment
4) Importance
5) Preventive measures
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Inspection: skin colour/integrity, calluses, ulcers, deformity, nail changes; check dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses; neuropathy: 10g monofilament test, vibration (128Hz tuning fork), ankle reflexes; importance: prevents amputation; prevention: daily foot inspection, proper footwear.
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Describe how you would grade the severity of the foot findings and decide on referral.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Grade per a foot-risk classification (e.g., low/moderate/high risk based on sensation, pulses, deformity, ulcer history); refer to podiatry/vascular surgery if high risk or active ulcer/pulse deficit.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss footwear and self-care advice you would counsel this patient on to prevent complications.

ospe.Title: Station 2
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: Newly diagnosed pulmonary TB patient.
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) Standard regimen
2) Adverse effects
3) Adherence importance
4) Infection control
5) Contact screening
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Regimen: 2HRZE/4HR under NTEP; adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy (INH), orange discolouration of secretions (Rifampicin), GI upset; adherence prevents drug resistance; infection control: cough etiquette, ventilation; contact screening: household contacts, especially children.
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Describe how you would counsel the patient on directly observed treatment (DOT) and manage a missed dose.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: DOT ensures each dose is directly observed; a missed dose should be taken as soon as remembered (or the missed dose rules under NTEP followed) and the patient counselled on adherence importance.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the notification and reporting requirements for this patient under the National TB Elimination Programme.

ospe.Title: Station 3
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: 32-week pregnant woman, routine ANC visit.
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) Abdominal exam steps
2) Leopold’s manoeuvres
3) Fundal height
4) FHR
5) Findings recorded
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Abdominal exam: inspection, palpation (fundal height, Leopold's 1st-4th manoeuvres), auscultation of FHR; fundal height should correspond to gestational age (~32cm at 32 weeks); FHR normal 110-160 bpm; findings recorded on ANC card/partograph.
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Describe how you would assess and record the lie, presentation, and engagement of the fetus.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Lie (longitudinal/transverse/oblique) via 1st/2nd manoeuvre; presentation (cephalic/breech) via 3rd manoeuvre; engagement via 4th manoeuvre (head fixed/free above pelvic brim).
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the antenatal danger signs you would counsel this mother to watch for and when to seek care.

ospe.Title: Station 4
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: 32-year-old woman choosing combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs).
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) When to start
2) Advantages
3) Side effects
4) Missed pills advice
5) STI prevention
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Start within first 5 days of menstrual cycle (or Quick Start with backup); advantages: highly effective, cycle regulation, reduces ovarian/endometrial cancer risk; side effects: nausea, breakthrough bleeding, weight change; missed pill: take as soon as remembered, backup contraception if >1 missed; does not protect against STIs.
ospe.Sub_Question_B: List the absolute and relative contraindications to combined oral contraceptive pills.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Absolute: pregnancy, history of thromboembolism, active liver disease, breast cancer, smokers >35 years; relative: hypertension, migraine with aura, diabetes with vascular disease.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss follow-up and switching advice if this method is discontinued or not tolerated.

ospe.Title: Station 5
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: 16-year-old boy, stray dog bite, lime applied to bleeding wound.
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) Exposure classification
2) Wound management
3) Vaccine schedule
4) RIG indications
5) Tetanus prophylaxis
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Category III exposure (bleeding wound with contact of saliva); wound management: wash with soap and water for 15 minutes, no local application of irritants; vaccine schedule: ID (Updated Thai Red Cross 2-2-2-0-2 or similar) vs IM (Essen 5-dose 0,3,7,14,28); RIG indicated for Category III exposure; tetanus per immunization status.
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Describe the intradermal vs intramuscular anti-rabies vaccination schedules and when each is used.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Intradermal regimen uses smaller vaccine volume at multiple sites (cost-effective, e.g., 2-site method); intramuscular regimen (Essen) is single-site, used where ID expertise/cold chain for multi-dose vials is unavailable.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the reporting and follow-up required for an animal-bite case under the National Rabies Control Programme.

ospe.Title: Station 6
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: 9-month-old child with some dehydration.
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) ORS dosage
2) Zinc dosage
3) Danger signs
4) Feeding advice
5) Immunization importance
ospe.Answer_Key_A: ORS ~75ml/kg over 4 hours; Zinc 10-20mg/day for 14 days; danger signs: unable to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy; feeding advice: continue breastfeeding/food; immunization importance: reduces diarrhoea-related complications (e.g., measles, rotavirus vaccination).
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Select the appropriate treatment plan (A/B/C) and describe it.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Classify as 'some dehydration' (Plan B per IMNCI signs) and initiate ORS + Zinc accordingly, with follow-up and referral if danger signs develop.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the counselling points for the caregiver on prevention of future diarrhoeal episodes.

ospe.Title: Station 7
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: Couple seeking contraceptive advice.
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) Temporary methods
2) Condom advantages
3) Contraindications to OCPs
4) Permanent methods advice
5) Dual protection
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Temporary methods: condoms, OCPs, IUCD, injectables; condom advantages: dual protection (pregnancy + STI/HIV), no hormonal side effects; OCP contraindications: thromboembolism history, smokers >35, liver disease; permanent methods: NSV/tubectomy after family completed; dual protection: condom use even with another method for STI prevention.
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Describe how you would counsel the couple on birth spacing before considering permanent methods.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Counsel on birth spacing (Cu-T, injectables) as temporary bridge before considering a permanent method once family size decisions are firmly made.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the follow-up schedule and side-effect monitoring you would advise for the chosen method.

ospe.Title: Station 8
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: 2-year-old child vaccinated only up to 14 weeks.
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) History regarding case
2) Catch-up immunization
3) Vaccines due
4) AEFI
ospe.Answer_Key_A: History: reason for interruption, illness/contraindications, AEFI history; catch-up: continue from where left off, no restart needed; vaccines due: age-appropriate remaining UIP doses; AEFI: recognize and manage minor/serious reactions.
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Describe how you would explain the catch-up schedule and counsel the parents on completing it.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Catch-up follows minimum-interval rules under UIP with no upper age limit for most antigens; explain this clearly to reassure parents there's no need to restart.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss how you would record and report this case in the immunization tracking system (Mother and Child Protection Card, U-WIN).

ospe.Title: Station 9
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: Plot
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) Identify
2) Uses
3) Other indicators
4) New standards
5) Colour coding
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Identify: standard WHO growth chart wt for age for girls; uses: monitor growth trend over time, early detection of faltering; other indicators: weight-for-age, height-for-age, MUAC; new WHO standards (2006) are based on breastfed reference population; colour coding: green (normal), yellow (caution), red (severely underweight/at risk).
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Describe how you would plot this child's measurement on the chart and classify the growth trend.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Plot weight/height against age on the correct sex-specific chart; classify trend as normal, static, or falling across centile lines (faltering growth).
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the counselling and referral steps you would take if the child's growth trend crosses a colour band.

ospe.Title: Station 10
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: Demonstrate knowledge of temperature monitoring and vaccine placement inside an Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR) at PHC
ospe.Sub_Question_A: State the recommended operating temperature range for an ILR.
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Specify which vaccines should be placed at the bottom shelf versus near the top of the ILR, and explain the rationale for this placement.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Freeze-sensitive vaccines (DPT, TT, HepB, Pentavalent, IPV) at the bottom, away from the evaporator; heat-sensitive but freeze-tolerant vaccines (BCG, OPV, Measles/MR) near the top/lid.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Describe the Shake Test procedure and its significance in detecting freeze damage in vaccines.

ospe.Title: Station 11
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: Perform estimation of chlorine demand for well having  100mtr depth of water and inner circumference of 6.28m water using Horrocks Apparatus.
ospe.Sub_Question_A:
1) Calculate the volume of water in the well from the given dimensions.
2) waiting time after adding bleaching powder solution
3) Name the indicator reagent used in the Horrocks Apparatus test and describe the colour change observed at the endpoint.
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Starch-iodide reagent or orthotolidine; a blue (starch-iodide) or canary yellow (orthotolidine) colour change indicates the endpoint (chlorine demand met).
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Calculate the bleaching powder requirement for this volume of water based on a cup reading showing a distinct colour change during the test.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: Bleaching powder requirement is calculated from the cup showing the first distinct colour change, scaled up proportionally to the total volume of water (455 litres) using the Horrocks Apparatus formula/table.
ospe.Sub_Question_C: State the recommended free residual chlorine level and the required contact time before it is measured.

ospe.Title: Station 12
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: A 28-year-old woman with known bronchial asthma comes to the PHC for a routine follow-up visit, complaining of mild breathlessness on exertion over the past week.
ospe.Sub_Question_A: 1) Demonstrate the correct technique for measuring Peak Expiratory Flow Rate using a peak flow meter. 2) State the precautions to be observed while taking the reading. 3) Explain how PEFR is used to classify asthma control. 4) State the expected predicted PEFR range for this patient's age, sex, and height.
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Technique: patient stands, takes a full breath in, seals lips around mouthpiece, blows out as hard and fast as possible in a single short blast; best of 3 attempts recorded. Precautions: reset the pointer before each attempt, ensure a tight lip seal, avoid coughing into the device, keep tongue clear of the mouthpiece. PEFR classification: Green zone (≥80% predicted/personal best) = good control; Yellow zone (50–79%) = caution, step up treatment; Red zone (<50%) = medical alert. Predicted PEFR for a 28-year-old woman is derived from standard nomograms based on age, sex, and height (typically ~400–450 L/min for average height).
ospe.Sub_Question_B: Describe how you would interpret a PEFR reading that falls in the "red zone" and the immediate management steps you would take.
ospe.Answer_Key_B: A red-zone reading (<50% of predicted/personal best) indicates a severe exacerbation. Immediate management: administer a short-acting bronchodilator (salbutamol) via nebulizer/inhaler with spacer, reassess PEFR after 15–20 minutes, give oral/systemic corticosteroids if no improvement, and refer/transport urgently if the patient remains in the red zone or shows danger signs (inability to speak in full sentences, cyanosis, silent chest).
ospe.Sub_Question_C: Discuss the role of a written asthma action plan and PEFR-based self-monitoring in long-term asthma control at the primary care level.

ospe.Title: Station 13
ospe.Scenario_or_Stem: A primigravida in active labor: Cervical dilation 4 cm at 8:00 AM, 5 cm at 12:00 PM crossing Alert Line.
ospe.Sub_Question_A: Define Alert Line and Action Line on WHO modified Partograph.
ospe.Answer_Key_A: Alert Line: plots expected cervical dilation of 1cm/hour from 4cm; crossing it signals slower-than-expected progress and need for closer monitoring. Action Line: drawn 4 hours to the right of the Alert Line; crossing it indicates the need for active intervention/referral.
